title: China's AI boom has left Nvidia and Anthropic on opposing sides
summary: China's AI advancements are causing divisions within Silicon Valley, leading to debates on U.S. response regarding access and competition; Anthropic advocates for restrictions due to alleged industrial espionage by Chinese firms.
scraped_content: The rapid rise of Chinese artificial intelligence has sparked an unusual divide inside Silicon Valley, pitting some of the world’s biggest AI developers against one another over how the United States should respond. Until recently, American companies were widely viewed as having an unassailable lead in frontier AI. But a string of increasingly capable Chinese models, including DeepSeek, Z.ai’s GLM 5.2 and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, has challenged that assumption. Many of these systems have delivered competitive performance while adopting an open-weight approach, allowing developers to download, modify and deploy the models on their own infrastructure. That shift has triggered a broader debate extending beyond technology and into national security, trade policy and intellectual property. At its centre is a simple question: should Washington restrict access to Chinese AI, or should US companies focus on building better alternatives? Anthropic has emerged as one of the strongest advocates for tighter controls. The Claude AI developer argues that several Chinese AI companies have narrowed the performance gap with American rivals not through independent breakthroughs, but by unlawfully extracting knowledge from frontier US models. “We have identified industrial-scale campaigns by three AI laboratories—DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax—to illicitly extract Claude’s capabilities to improve their own models,” Anthropic said. According to the company, those organisations generated more than 16 million interactions with Claude using approximately 24,000 fraudulent accounts, allegedly breaching its terms of service and regional access restrictions.
